title: Hanuman's empty seat
hookLine: an empty seat at a Ramayana reading, and the listener tradition says never misses it
carry: shravana: hearing god's story is devotion
tomorrow: if one wrong sound can spoil a mantra, what about a sincere heart?

cards: At many Ramayana readings, in temples and in living rooms, there's a strange detail. The reader sits. The families sit.
And one seat, often with a cloth or a flower on it, stays empty the whole time. No one takes it, not even when the room is packed. Kids try, and get waved off by three aunties at once.
Nobody is late. Nobody is expected. So who is that seat for?

teach.b: It's for Hanuman. Here's why. Near the end of the Ramayana, as Rama prepares to leave the earth, Hanuman asks for something unusual.

teach.h: AS LONG AS RAMA'S STORY IS TOLD.
teach.b: In Valmiki's telling, he asks to stay alive in the world for as long as Rama's story is told among people, and Rama grants it. So Hindus count Hanuman among the chiranjivis, the long-lived ones still in the world.
And an old verse sung to him says where to find him: wherever Rama's name and glory are sung, there is Hanuman, palms joined above his head, eyes full of tears. That's the empty seat.
The story is being told, so the greatest listener has come. Under the custom sits a big teaching.

Hindus call it shravana, hearing: listening to God's story is itself a form of devotion, the first in the Bhagavata's list of nine. You don't have to be the reader. You don't have to catch every word.

teach.h: THE SEAT IS FOR THE LISTENER.
teach.b: Sitting and hearing the story is the practice.
It's why families gather for katha, a holy story told aloud, why in Kerala many homes read the Ramayana through in one month each year, and why grandparents tell the same stories again and again.
Hanuman, strongest of all, chose to spend forever listening.

how: At many Ramayana readings and katha gatherings a seat is left empty for Hanuman, and listening to the sacred story, shravana, is counted as devotion in itself.

games.why: in Valmiki's telling, Hanuman asked to live as long as Rama's story is told. many families keep him a seat, because hearing the story is devotion.

practice: Bring to mind a story you love of Rama, Krishna, Shiva or the Goddess, and tell it to yourself in a few lines, slowly, as if someone were listening beside you. If you pray, end with Rama's name.
If you don't, just notice how a story you love feels when you hear it again. Then rest with the breath.
